archetype.name: Playoff Team (goalie-and-special-teams)
archetype.definition: A club that wins with its goaltending, its kills and a power play built around two stars, while breaking roughly even at 5-on-5. That is the same profile that carried Minnesota to a top-seven site finish last season.

report.headline: Wallstedt and the special teams are winning games that 5-on-5 play only splits
report.take:
Seven games in, Minnesota looks a lot like last season. The Wild ranked 4th in Def Rank in 2025-26 and sit 4th again now. The Goalies GSAx is positive again, and the 5-on-5 shares sit right around even. That is why a 4-2-1 record with a +0.71 Goal Diff / GP lands them 6th on the Teams tab. It is a known identity, not a hot start from nowhere. The margin comes from three places: the crease, the penalty kill and a power play converting at a league-best 36.8%.

The goaltending is the foundation. Jesper Wallstedt has started six of seven games with a .933 Save %, a 1.82 GAA and 6.9 GSAx, good for 4th on the goalie tab. His lone start off came from Calvin Pickard, who posted -2.2 GSAx in that game. The drop-off behind the starter is steep. Up front, Kirill Kaprizov is the top left wing on the site with 8 goals on 20 shots, and Quinn Hughes is the No. 2 defenseman with 10 points while logging nearly 27 minutes a night. The forwards' listed group has 13 of its 31 points on the power play. That reliance on special teams is the pattern to keep an eye on.

The 5-on-5 numbers are flatter than the record. Minnesota owns 49.7% of expected goals (20th) and 50% of shot attempts (16th). The Eriksson Ek–Boldy–Kaprizov core is clearly winning its minutes, all near or above 60% xGF. The rest of the lineup is giving those minutes back. Ryan Hartman is at a .343 xGF share and -7, Yakov Trenin has no points, and the third pair of Zach Bogosian and Daemon Hunt are both under 40%. That is why the blueline grades a C even with Hughes on it.

The record isn't flattering them, though. Pts vs Goal Diff is slightly negative, and PDO is 98.4. That suggests 5-on-5 finishing has run cold even with Wallstedt stopping everything. Some regression on the power play is near certain. Some recovery at even strength is plausible. The net is a team that should keep winning more than it loses, driven by the same formula as last year.

strengths.title: Wallstedt is stealing goals
strengths.body: Wallstedt's 6.9 GSAx accounts for more than the whole team figure, since Pickard's one start was below expected. This is the main reason the defense ranks 4th despite middling shot and chance shares. A goalie this far above expected will cool somewhat, but the franchise has posted positive team GSAx in recent seasons and he has the tab rank to back it.

strengths.title: Elite special teams on both ends
strengths.body: The power play leads the league and the kill ranks 4th. Kaprizov, Hughes, Coleman and Shabanov are all piling up PP points. At 36.8%, the power play will come down; no unit sustains that. The kill was solid last season too, so a top-ten finish there is realistic.

strengths.title: Two stars carrying the top line
strengths.body: Kaprizov ranks 1st among left wings and Hughes 2nd among defensemen, and both are well above 55% in expected-goal share. Their production is real driving of play, not just power-play padding. Kaprizov's goal pace on his shot volume will slow, but his line's chance share supports continued scoring.

concerns.title: Even-strength play is only break-even
concerns.body: A 49.7% xGF share ranks 20th, which is closer to a bubble team than a top-six one. Minnesota has run at or below 50% in several recent seasons and relied on goaltending to cover it. That works until the goalie or the power play has an off month.

concerns.title: Depth forwards and third pair bleed chances
concerns.body: Hartman and Trenin are getting crushed in their minutes. Bogosian and Hunt sit near the bottom of the defenseman tab. These players account for a large chunk of the ice time outside the top unit, and they explain the C blueline grade around Hughes.

concerns.title: Thin behind Wallstedt
concerns.body: Pickard's one start produced a 5.00 GAA. With Wallstedt carrying six of seven starts, any fatigue or injury to him exposes the weakest part of the depth chart.

trend.note: The first seven games alternated pairs of wins and losses, with no streak longer than two either way. Minnesota has generally won comfortably and lost close or on the road, ending the stretch with a 5-2 loss in Winnipeg.

weekAhead.headline: Two home games against leaky defenses, then a trip to Edmonton
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with St. Louis and Columbus at home, and both are softer than Minnesota in the ways that matter here. The Blues actually out-chance opponents, with a 55.1% xGF share that ranks 7th. But their power play ranks 25th, which blunts the one area where they could punish Minnesota's depth. Their goalies are below expected. Columbus is 27th on the site, with the 29th-ranked defense, a 61.1% penalty kill and goaltending graded D-. That is a near-ideal matchup for a league-best power play.

The road finale in Edmonton is the real test. The Oilers are 5-0-1, but a 109.1 PDO and a league-high Pts vs Goal Diff say that record is running hot. Their 73.7% kill and below-expected goaltending offer openings. A 2-1 week is the baseline, and a sweep is realistic if the power play travels.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota power play vs. Columbus kill
keyMatchups.body: The league's best power play meets a kill ranked 29th behind a defense ranked 29th. Columbus has also allowed the most points to wingers relative to expectation. That plays straight into Kaprizov and Boldy. This is the game to bank.

keyMatchups.title: Blues' 5-on-5 edge vs. Wallstedt
keyMatchups.body: St. Louis owns the better 5-on-5 chance share in this matchup. If the Wild's depth lines get pinned, Wallstedt will have to steal another one. The Blues' weak power play means Minnesota can afford to play physical.

keyMatchups.title: Edmonton's hot start meets regression
keyMatchups.body: The Oilers lead the league in Goal Diff / GP with the 2nd-ranked offense. But their PDO and Pts vs Goal Diff point to bounces, and their kill ranks 26th. A disciplined road game that gets Minnesota onto the power play is the path to a win.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the non-Kaprizov lines can hold their own at 5-on-5 against St. Louis. That is the clearest read on whether this team needs its power play every night.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the power play to fall from its league-leading pace toward merely good, and expect Wallstedt's save rate to settle somewhat. The defense-first identity should hold. It has been there in multiple recent seasons, and the goalie and the kill are the most repeatable parts of this profile. Offsetting some of the regression, the slightly negative Pts vs Goal Diff and a sub-100 PDO suggest even-strength finishing and close-game results have room to improve.

The ceiling depends on depth. If the bottom six and third pair can get closer to even in chance share, this is a top-eight team again. If not, it is a playoff team that lives on Wallstedt and Kaprizov and is vulnerable whenever either cools.
swingFactors: How far the power play regresses

confidence.note: Only seven games of data. History backs the defense-and-goaltending identity, but the special-teams rates are small-sample.
